Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Remibrutinib is a highly selective, potent, covalent, CNS-penetrant, oral BTK inhibitor. We assessed the efficacy and safety of remibrutinib in adult patients with relapsing multiple sclerosis. METHODS: REMODEL-1 and REMODEL-2 are two identical, randomised, double-blind, double-dummy, active comparator-controlled, parallel-group, event-driven, phase 3 trials conducted at 407 centres in 46 countries. Patients aged 18-55 years with relapsing multiple sclerosis, an Expanded Disability Status Scale score of 0-5·5, and evidence of recent disease activity were randomly assigned 1:1 to oral remibrutinib 100 mg twice daily or teriflunomide 14 mg once daily via interactive response technology. Randomisation was stratified by geographical region, MRI cohort participation, and multiple sclerosis subtype. Patients, site investigators, and trial team were masked to treatment allocation. The primary endpoint was annualised relapse rate (ARR), defined as the number of confirmed multiple sclerosis relapses per patient-year with up to 30 months of follow-up, and assessed in all randomly assigned patients. These trials are registered with ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT05147220 and NCT05156281) and are ongoing, not recruiting. FINDINGS: Between Dec 13, 2021, and Dec 30, 2025, 2632 patients were screened and 2007 patients were randomly assigned. REMODEL-1 included 1000 patients (remibrutinib 502, teriflunomide 498; mean age 38·2 years, 666 [66·6%] female, 334 [33·4%] male) and REMODEL-2 included 1007 patients (remibrutinib 504, teriflunomide 503; mean age 39·0 years, 675 [67·0%] female, 332 [33·0%] male). ARR was significantly lower with remibrutinib than with teriflunomide: 0·073 versus 0·112 (rate ratio [RR] 0·648 [95% CI 0·453-0·927]; p=0·018) in REMODEL-1 and 0·080 versus 0·116 (RR 0·688 [0·487-0·972]; p=0·034) in REMODEL-2. The most common adverse events were upper respiratory tract infection (132 [13·1%] of 1006 with remibrutinib vs 137 [13·7%] of 1001 with teriflunomide), nasopharyngitis (92 [9·1%] vs 123 [12·3%]), diarrhoea (84 [8·3%] vs 109 [10·9%]), and alopecia (58 [5·8%] vs 135 [13·5%]). Adverse events leading to treatment discontinuation were less frequent with remibrutinib (31 [3·1%]) versus teriflunomide (58 [5·8%]). The safety profile of remibrutinib was consistent with that in other indications, including no liver safety concerns. INTERPRETATION: Remibrutinib was superior to teriflunomide in patients with relapsing multiple sclerosis, while maintaining a favourable safety profile. These findings support remibrutinib as a potential new oral treatment option for relapsing multiple sclerosis. FUNDING: Novartis.

item.title: Perioperative chemotherapy and stereotactic body radiotherapy versus perioperative chemotherapy alone in patients with high-risk, localised pancreatic cancer (MASTERPLAN): an open-label, phase 2, multicentre, randomised trial of the Australasian Gastro-Intestinal Trials Group.
item.dc:creator: Oar A, Kneebone A, Sjoquist KM, Espinoza D, Lee M, Le H, Gholamrezaei L, Chu J, Lynam J, Mallesara G, et al.
item.description:
Authors: Oar A, Kneebone A, Sjoquist KM, Espinoza D, Lee M, Le H, Gholamrezaei L, Chu J, Lynam J, Mallesara G, et al.
Journal: The Lancet. Oncology | DOI: 10.1016/S1470-2045(26)00532-2
Published: 2026-Oct-23
PMID: 42914998



Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) has poor outcomes and high rates of locoregional recurrence. MASTERPLAN evaluated whether stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT) reduced locoregional recurrence in patients with high-risk, localised PDAC. METHODS: MASTERPLAN was an open-label, randomised, phase 2 trial conducted across 14 hospitals in Australia and New Zealand. Eligible participants were aged 18 years or older with an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status of 0-1, and had previously untreated localised PDAC with at least one high-risk feature, including tumour size more than 4 cm, extrapancreatic extension, node-positive disease, borderline resectable disease, or locally advanced disease. Participants were randomly assigned (2:1) using the method of minimisation to investigator-choice chemotherapy, with or without SBRT, stratified by participant cohort (potentially operable vs inoperable), planned chemotherapy regimen, randomisation before or within the first 28 days of chemotherapy, and institution. Chemotherapy consisted of mFOLFIRINOX (day 1 oxaliplatin 85 mg/m2, irinotecan 150 mg/m2, leucovorin 50 mg, and fluorouracil 2400 mg/m2 over 46 h every 14 days for six cycles; all intravenous) or gemcitabine plus nab-paclitaxel (gemcitabine 1000 mg/m2 and nab-paclitaxel 125 mg/m2 on days 1, 8, and 15 every 28 days for three cycles; both intravenous). SBRT was delivered as 40 Gy in five fractions, with two to four fractions delivered per week, with real-time radiotherapy quality assurance. Surgical resection was considered following induction therapy, followed by a planned further 12 weeks of adjuvant chemotherapy with either mFOLFIRINOX or gemcitabine plus capecitabine (28-day cycles of 1000 mg/m2 intravenous gemcitabine administered on days 1, 8, and 15 with 830 mg/m2 oral capecitabine twice daily administered on days 1-21). Participants deemed not suitable for surgery continued the same chemotherapy for an additional 12 weeks with reassessment for surgical suitability permitted, for a total planned duration of chemotherapy of 24 weeks. The primary endpoint was 12-month locoregional recurrence in the intention-to-treat population, with safety endpoints analysed by treatment received. The trial planned to recruit 120 patients but due to slow accrual closed to recruitment early on Jan 6, 2025. Trial closure and database lock occurred on July 21, 2026. This trial was registered with the Australian New Zealand Clinical Trial Registry (ACTRN12619000409178) and ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT04089150), and is complete. FINDINGS: Between Feb 26, 2020, and Jan 6, 2025, 74 participants (43 [58%] male, 31 [42%] female) were randomly assigned to chemotherapy and SBRT (n=49) or chemotherapy alone (n=25). After a median follow-up of 3·2 years (IQR 1·9-4·3), 12-month locoregional recurrence was 20·2% (95% CI 9·9-33·1) in the SBRT group and 52·0% (30·3-69·9) in the chemotherapy alone group (subdistribution hazard ratio 0·44 [95% CI 0·22-0·88]; p=0·022). Grade 3 or higher adverse events occurred in 33 (70%) of 47 participants in the SBRT group and 16 (64%) of 25 participants in the chemotherapy alone group (p=0·27), with one (4%) treatment-related death secondary to biliary tract infection in the chemotherapy alone group. The most common grade 3-4 adverse events were diarrhoea (seven [15%] in the SBRT group vs five [20%] in the chemotherapy alone group), and thromboembolic events (three [6%]) vs one [4%]). Overall grade 3 or higher serious adverse events occurred in 30 (64%) of 47 participants in the SBRT group, and 14 (56%) of 25 participants in the chemotherapy alone group (p=0·24). There were two serious adverse events attributable to SBRT; grade 2 small bowel obstruction and grade 3 pancreatitis. INTERPRETATION: In patients with high-risk, localised PDAC, the addition of SBRT to chemotherapy was associated with significantly reduced locoregional recurrence without a significant increase in toxicity and warrants further investigation in larger studies. FUNDING: Medical Research Future Fund, Australasian Gastro-Intestinal Trials Group, National Health and Medical Research Council Clinical Trials Centre (University of Sydney), and Gut Cancer Foundation, New Zealand.

item.title: Head and neck cancer incidence and two-year mortality in Aotearoa New Zealand, 2009-2020: a national population-based cohort study.
item.dc:creator: Chauhan AS, Davie G, Barson D, Parackal SM, Russell-Camp T, Wong A
item.description:
Authors: Chauhan AS, Davie G, Barson D, Parackal SM, Russell-Camp T, Wong A
Journal: Cancer epidemiology | DOI: 10.1016/j.canep.2026.103264
Published: 2026-Oct-23
PMID: 42914788



Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Head and neck cancer (HNC) imposes a substantial burden in Aotearoa New Zealand (AoNZ), yet contemporary population-level data on incidence and early mortality across sociodemographic groups remain limited. METHODS: This population-based retrospective cohort study used New Zealand Cancer Registry to identify all primary HNC diagnoses from 2009 to 2020 (n = 6980). The cases were classified according to ICD-10 subsites. Incidence rates (IRs), age-standardised IRs, and age-standardised rate ratios were estimated by age, sex, ethnicity, socioeconomic deprivation, and rurality. Regression models were used to estimate annual percentage change in IRs and to estimate adjusted risk ratios for two-year all-cause mortality. RESULTS: In total 6980 people were diagnosed with HNC; an overall incidence rate of 13.5 per 100,000 person-years (PY). Oropharyngeal cancer (OPC), the most common subsite, increased from 3.4 per 100,000 PY in 2009-2011-4.9 per 100,000 PY in 2018-2020, whereas IRs for oral cavity cancer (OCC), the second most common, were more stable. HNC IRs were higher among males, older adults, Māori, Pacific Peoples and people living in the most socioeconomically deprived areas, with subsite-specific differences: Māori experienced higher OPC incidence rates, while Pacific Peoples experienced higher OCC IRs. Within two years of diagnosis, 25.2% of patients had died. Two-year all-cause mortality was 44.4% for hypopharyngeal cancer, 30.9% for OCC, and 22.7% for OPC. Among people diagnosed with HNC, after adjusting for available sociodemographic factors and treatment timing, two-year all-cause mortality was higher for Māori, Pacific Peoples, and those in the most deprived quintile. Rurality showed no consistent association with incidence or two-year mortality. CONCLUSIONS: These findings indicate an OPC-driven shift in HNC epidemiology in AoNZ and a persistent inequitable burden of both disease occurrence and early mortality, supporting stronger surveillance and equity-focused cancer-control responses.

item.title: Precancerous cervical lesions and associated factors among HIV-positive women in Southern and Eastern African countries: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
item.dc:creator: Alemu GG, Bazezew AM, Yirsaw AN, Wondie WT, Mengistie BA, Dagnaw TE, Aweke MN, Baykemagn ND, Lakew G, Gebretsadkan BT
item.description:
Authors: Alemu GG, Bazezew AM, Yirsaw AN, Wondie WT, Mengistie BA, Dagnaw TE, Aweke MN, Baykemagn ND, Lakew G, Gebretsadkan BT
Journal: PloS one | DOI: 10.1371/journal.pone.0361185
Published: 2026-01-01
PMID: 42912824



Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Women living with HIV (WLHIV) face a sixfold increased risk of cervical cancer compared to HIV-negative women. Most WLHIV residing in the Southern and Eastern African regions have a substantial HIV-related cervical cancer burden. Studies on precancerous cervical lesions (PCCL) and associated factors in WLHIV from these regions have inconsistent and inconclusive findings. Therefore, we aimed to synthesize the pooled prevalence of PCCL and associated factors among WLHIV in Southern and Eastern Africa. METHODS: This study was registered under PROSPERO (CRD420251123583) and conducted in accordance with PRISMA 2020 standards. Primary studies published from inception to 2025 in Southern and Eastern Africa were included. The methodological quality of studies was assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa scale. Data extraction and statistical analyses were done in Microsoft Excel and STATA 17, respectively. Pooled prevalence, publication bias, subgroup, and sensitivity analysis were conducted. Associations were expressed as odds ratios (OR), and a p-value of less than 0.05 was considered statistically significant. RESULTS: 44 studies met the inclusion criteria, with a sample size of 47,009. The pooled prevalence of PCCL was 22.25% (95% CI: 19.57, 24.93). Age at first sexual intercourse (< 18 years) (OR = 2.99, (2.34, 3.82)), multiparity (OR = 4.97, (3.21, 7.69)), having multiple sexual partners (OR = 3.06 (2.45, 3.83)), having a history of sexually transmitted infections (STI) (OR = 3.93 (3.23, 4.78)), smoking (OR = 7.01, (3.39, 14.49)), ever taking oral contraceptive pills (OR = 2.69, (1.85, 3.90)), low CD4 count (OR = 1.79, (1.56, 2.05)), and having not initiated antiretroviral therapy (ART) (OR = 2.02, (1.56, 2.62)) were significantly associated with an increased risk of PCCL. CONCLUSION AND RECOMMENDATIONS: The pooled prevalence of PCCL was high. Additionally, early first sexual intercourse, parity, STIs, multiple sexual partners, smoking, oral contraceptive use, CD4 count, and ART were positively associated with the occurrence of PCCL. Therefore, stakeholders shall implement interventions to avert future incidents of PCCL and address the identified factors.

item.title: Do community pharmacies unnecessarily recommend oral emergency contraception? A nationwide mystery caller investigation in Germany.
item.dc:creator: Langer B, Beck A, Dreier AM, Gabrieljan R, Hilgenhof H, Latuske J, Priepke C, Schaihadinow K, Schwarz H, Kunow C
item.description:
Authors: Langer B, Beck A, Dreier AM, Gabrieljan R, Hilgenhof H, Latuske J, Priepke C, Schaihadinow K, Schwarz H, Kunow C
Journal: PloS one | DOI: 10.1371/journal.pone.0361027
Published: 2026-01-01
PMID: 42912737



Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Since 2015, oral emergency contraceptives (ECs) have been available in German community pharmacies without prescription as over-the-counter medicines. Given the financial burden, unnecessary hormonal exposure and associated side effects, systematic information gathering is crucial to prevent unnecessary recommendations. This study aimed to determine whether pharmacy staff ask the checklist questions recommended by the German Federal Chamber of Pharmacists (BAK) guideline and provide correct recommendations when oral EC is not indicated (appropriate outcome), and to examine associated factors. METHODS: A nationwide study using the simulated patient methodology - considered the "gold standard" - was conducted with a stratified random sample of 376 community pharmacies across Germany. Eight trained female mystery callers aged 21-24 simulated a scenario in which a combined oral contraceptive was forgotten once after sexual intercourse. However, the pill could still be taken within the 12-hour window, making oral EC unnecessary according to the BAK guideline. To ensure quality, each call was monitored by a second observer. RESULTS: Of 376 mystery calls conducted, 322 were included in the primary analysis. An appropriate outcome was achieved in 44.4% (143/322), while oral EC was unnecessarily recommended in 49.1% (158/322). The median questioning score was 2.0 of 4.0 points. A multivariable logistic regression model showed that a higher questioning score and mystery caller identity were significantly associated with the appropriate outcome. Qualitative findings indicated both positive counseling practices and notable deficiencies among pharmacy staff. CONCLUSION: The results show deficits in information gathering and appropriate recommendations. To improve counseling, the consistent use of the BAK checklist during telephone consultations should be explicitly recommended in the relevant guideline. Targeted training for pharmacy staff may help address professional and communication deficits. Surprisingly, some mystery callers were significantly associated with the appropriate outcome, highlighting the need for further research on the influence of vocal characteristics and last names in telephone consultations.

item.title: Pharmacokinetic diversity of baloxavir marboxil across rare avian species.
item.dc:creator: Shimazu Y, Obara RD, Miki M, Osaki H, Yoshimoto Y, Hayashi M, Toyoda K, Ozaki M, Hanada I, Matsumoto R, et al.
item.description:
Authors: Shimazu Y, Obara RD, Miki M, Osaki H, Yoshimoto Y, Hayashi M, Toyoda K, Ozaki M, Hanada I, Matsumoto R, et al.
Journal: PloS one | DOI: 10.1371/journal.pone.0361119
Published: 2026-01-01
PMID: 42912701



Abstract:
High pathogenicity avian influenza virus (HPAIV) poses a serious threat to captive rare birds. Because effective countermeasures are limited, the use of human antiviral drugs to treat HPAIV infections in captive rare birds has been considered. Although the human antiviral drug, baloxavir marboxil (BXM), is not approved for the treatment of influenza virus infection in birds, previous studies demonstrated the antiviral efficacy of BXM in experimental avian models. Pharmacokinetic studies have also revealed substantial interspecies differences following BXM administration, suggesting the need to establish species-specific dosing regimens. In this study, BXM was administered to 14 avian species to optimize dosing regimens for each species. Oral administration of BXM using different methods revealed that drug-food interactions had a limited impact on systemic drug exposure. Pharmacokinetic analysis of BXM and its active metabolite, baloxavir acid (BXA), demonstrated marked interspecies variability in drug exposure, contributing to the development of optimized dosing regimens for each species. Furthermore, systemic exposure to BXA was strongly associated with drug absorption indicators, suggesting that species-specific differences in absorption efficiency largely determine BXA exposure among avian species. This study provides a pharmacokinetic basis for the rational use of BXM in diverse avian species. It contributes to the development of practical antiviral strategies to protect captive rare birds against HPAIVs.

item.title: Why Are We Doing Pediatric Parotid Surgery? Insights From a Tertiary Center's Experience.
item.dc:creator: Barham D, Brennan L, Stobbs N
item.description:
Authors: Barham D, Brennan L, Stobbs N
Journal: The Laryngoscope | DOI: 10.1002/lary.71013
Published: 2026-Oct-22
PMID: 42919110



Abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To establish common clinicopathological themes of pediatric parotidectomy, aid decision making, and compare this to previously reported features and outcomes. METHODS: Retrospective cohort analysis of all pediatric parotidectomies over a 10-year period at a tertiary level pediatric hospital. RESULTS: Thirty-one patients were identified (15 male, 16 female) between the ages of 1 and 16. Primary parotid tumor was the most common reason for surgery (n = 15), followed by congenital abnormalities (n = 12). The most common histopathological diagnosis was acinic cell carcinoma (n = 6). The most common complication was temporary facial nerve weakness (29%). CONCLUSION: Primary parotid tumors were the most common reason for parotidectomy, and most of these were malignant. Of these, Acinic Cell Carcinoma was more prevalent than Mucoepidermoid Carcinoma. Pediatric parotidectomy is safe with a low permanent complication rate, but patients should be specifically counseled about temporary facial nerve weakness and the small risk of permanent injury.

item.title: Sexual dysfunction in men after radiotherapy for squamous cell carcinoma of the Anus: A danish anal cancer group DACG study.
item.dc:creator: Krogstrup MJ, Steffensen JH, Serup-Hansen E, Kronborg C, Spindler KG
item.description:
Authors: Krogstrup MJ, Steffensen JH, Serup-Hansen E, Kronborg C, Spindler KG
Journal: Radiotherapy and oncology : journal of the European Society for Therapeutic Radiology and Oncology | DOI: 10.1016/j.radonc.2026.111850
Published: 2026-Oct-22
PMID: 42913945



Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Sexual dysfunction, particularly erectile dysfunction (ED), is well documented after pelvic radiotherapy, but evidence in men with squamous cell carcinoma of the anus (SCCA) remains sparse. PURPOSE: To assess erectile and ejaculatory function, and sexual interest up to five years after curative-intent radiotherapy for SCCA, based on physician-graded toxicity and validated patient-reported outcomes (PROs). METHODS: This sub-study of the prospective DACG-I cohort (NCT05570279) included men treated with curative-intent radiotherapy for SCCA (2015-2020). PROs (EORTC QLQ-C30 and QLQ-CR29) and physician-graded toxicity (CTCAE v4.0) were collected at baseline, 1, 3, and 5-years. Symptom prevalences were described descriptively. Longitudinal changes were assessed using linear mixed-effects models on linearly transformed EORTC scores. RESULTS: Of 80 enrolled men, baseline data were available for 76. At baseline, majority were symptom-free. Erectile and ejaculatory dysfunction emerged mainly within 1-3 years after treatment and persisted through 5 years. For the total cohort, ejaculatory dysfunction increased from 4.5% at baseline to 12.3% at 3 years. Physician-assessed ED (NCI-CTCAE grade ≥ 2) increased from 11.9% to 39.3% at 3 years. PROs indicated greater deterioration in erectile function at parallel time points. EORTC scores confirmed moderate-to-major clinically important deterioration at 1 and 3 years. Sexual interest remained stable over time. CONCLUSION: Sexual dysfunction, particularly ED, represents an increasingly prevalent and persistent late adverse effect in men treated with curative-intent radiotherapy for SCCA. The early onset of symptoms and the limited extent of recovery underscore the need for structured assessment based on PROs to support timely identification and supportive care.

item.title: Consensus on current clinical workflow and future use of 3D models in parotid gland tumor surgery: A Delphi study.
item.dc:creator: Moll MCM, Karssemakers LHE, Braun LMM, van Alphen MJA, Valstar MH, Smeele LE, Zuur CL, Arends CR
item.description:
Authors: Moll MCM, Karssemakers LHE, Braun LMM, van Alphen MJA, Valstar MH, Smeele LE, Zuur CL, Arends CR
Journal: Oral oncology | DOI: 10.1016/j.oraloncology.2026.108163
Published: 2026-Oct-22
PMID: 42913203



Abstract:
OBJECTIVE: MRI-based 3D models provide patient-specific spatial information on the relationship between parotid gland tumors and the facial nerve. However, their potential role in clinical practice and the level of support for their implementation remain unclear. This study aimed to assess the level of consensus among surgeons on the current clinical workflows in parotid gland surgery and the future role of 3D models. STUDY DESIGN: We used a three-round Delphi study to explore consensus among surgeons performing more than five parotid surgeries annually. Round 1 consisted of semi-structured interviews about parotid surgery, innovations, and the use of 3D models. Inductive analysis was used to formulate statements and questions for round 2. In rounds 2 and 3, participants rated the questions and statements on a 7-point adjective scale. RESULTS: A panel of 15 surgeons, including 9 otolaryngologists and 6 oral and maxillofacial surgeons from nine Dutch hospitals, completed all study rounds. Partial consensus was observed for 10% of statements in round 3. Trends toward greater importance of both MRI scanning and 3D model use were identified in cases involving malignancy, facial nerve dysfunction, deep lobe tumors, fixed tumors, non-palpable tumors, and indications for a mastoidectomy. Stronger trends toward importance were observed for using 3D models in preoperative planning and patient counseling than in their use during surgery. CONCLUSION: Although consensus was limited, this study identified indications for MRI use and highlighted the perceived value of 3D models in parotid gland tumor surgery.

item.title: The 5-mm margin in head and neck cancer surgery: From uncontrolled historical dogma to personalised surgery.
item.dc:creator: Roussel LM, Berghian A, Hapdey S, Clatot F
item.description:
Authors: Roussel LM, Berghian A, Hapdey S, Clatot F
Journal: Oral oncology | DOI: 10.1016/j.oraloncology.2026.108194
Published: 2026-Oct-22
PMID: 42913202



Abstract:
For decades, a histological margin of 5 mm has been used as the practical definition of a "clear" resection in Head and Neck squamous cell carcinoma, particularly in the oral cavity. This short communication revisits the origins of this threshold, ang argues that it is based more on historical convention than on true validation of oncological biology. Although retrospective studies and meta-analyses have reinforced the 5 mm rule, their interpretation is limited by treatment-selection bias since adjuvant radiotherapy was systematically delivered to patients whose margins fell below this value. Furthermore, the 5 mm definition does not consider how residual disease spreads. Available data suggest that front morphology, as determined by the worst pattern of invasion and tumour budding, is associated with the margin width, even though this needs to be confirmed prospectively. Rather than replacing margin distance, which remains clinically useful and validated, these factors could complement it. Integrating these factors into therapeutic decision-making could be a promising way to achieve personalised management.

item.title: Monthly high-dose cholecalciferol supplementation in prostate cancer patients (ProsD trial): A nested analysis of vitamin D metabolites, metabolic ratios, and biochemical safety.
item.dc:creator: Tan C, David MC, Anderson PH, Mason RS, Fraser DR, Kimlin MG, Sawyer RK, Amirmostofian M, Frydenberg M, Yaxley JW, et al.
item.description:
Authors: Tan C, David MC, Anderson PH, Mason RS, Fraser DR, Kimlin MG, Sawyer RK, Amirmostofian M, Frydenberg M, Yaxley JW, et al.
Journal: Cancer epidemiology | DOI: 10.1016/j.canep.2026.103258
Published: 2026-Oct-22
PMID: 42913061



Abstract:
BACKGROUND: The effects of intermittent, high-dose cholecalciferol supplementation on circulating vitamin D metabolites and related biomarkers remain unclear. The ProsD randomised controlled trial evaluated the effects of monthly oral supplementation with 50,000 IU cholecalciferol in males with prostate cancer and assessed longitudinal changes in vitamin D metabolite responses. OBJECTIVE: To characterise vitamin D metabolites and ratios after a monthly dose of 50,000 IU cholecalciferol supplementation and to assess the effects on biochemical markers. METHODS: ProsD recruited and randomised 123 men with prostate cancer; 118 participants (placebo n = 40; vitamin D n = 78) provided blood samples at baseline, and from remaining participants at 0, 6, 12, and 24 months, at follow-up visits. Plasma vitamin D metabolites-25(OH)D3, 1,25(OH)2D3, 24,25(OH)2D3, and 3-epi-25(OH)D3-and vitamin D metabolite ratios (VMRs) were quantified. Longitudinal changes and between-group differences were evaluated using age-adjusted generalised estimating equations with estimated marginal means. Routine biochemical markers were also assessed. RESULTS: Compared with placebo, monthly cholecalciferol supplementation increased peak between-group difference at 24 months for 25(OH)D3 (+30.10 nmol/L; p < 0.01), 1,25(OH)2D3 (+12.44 pmol/L; p = 0.11), 24,25(OH)2D3 (+3.95 nmol/L; p < 0.01), and 3-epi-25(OH)D3 (+5.94 nmol/L; p < 0.01). The 25(OH)D3:24,25(OH)2D3 VMR increased in the placebo group but remained constant in the intervention group, and between-group analysis showed consistently lower ratios in the vitamin D group. All routine biomarkers remained within normal ranges throughout follow-up. CONCLUSIONS: Monthly oral supplementation of 50,000 IU cholecalciferol in men with prostate cancer produced sustained increases across multiple vitamin D metabolites over 24 months, accompanied by adaptive shifts in metabolite ratios consistent with regulated catabolic activation, with no clinically meaningful abnormalities in biochemical markers. item.title: 630 nm light-emitting diode irradiation suppresses inflammation and promotes osteoblast differentiation in periodontal cell models - in vitro study.
item.dc:creator: Lee JK, Lee MS, Jeong JH, Ahn SH
item.description:
Authors: Lee JK, Lee MS, Jeong JH, Ahn SH
Journal: PloS one | DOI: 10.1371/journal.pone.0351995
Published: 2026-01-01
PMID: 42911963



Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Periodontal disease involves persistent inflammation and alveolar bone loss. Photobiomodulation using light-emitting diodes (LEDs) may regulate inflammation and bone remodelling, but the optimal wavelength and irradiation timing remain unclear. METHODS: Human gingival fibroblasts and RAW 264.7 macrophages were irradiated with 525, 630, or 850 nm LED light before or after lipopolysaccharide (LPS) stimulation. The effects of 630 nm irradiation were further evaluated in primary mouse calvarial osteoblasts, MC3T3-E1 cells, bone marrow-derived macrophages, and RAW 264.7 osteoclast precursors. Inflammatory mediators, nitric oxide production, cell viability, osteoblast differentiation, and osteoclast formation were assessed. RESULTS: Among the wavelengths tested, 630 nm irradiation most consistently reduced pro-inflammatory cytokine expression and secretion and decreased nitric oxide production without affecting cell viability. In primary osteoblasts and MC3T3-E1 cells, 630 nm irradiation at 5 and 10 J/cm² increased alkaline phosphatase (ALP) activity, osteogenic marker expression, RUNX2 protein levels, and Smad1/5/9 phosphorylation. In contrast, the same irradiation conditions did not significantly affect osteoclast differentiation or the expression of osteoclast-related markers. CONCLUSION: Irradiation with 630 nm LED light suppressed inflammatory responses and promoted osteoblast differentiation without enhancing osteoclastogenesis. These findings suggest that 630 nm photobiomodulation may provide a balanced therapeutic approach for periodontal disease, although further validation in animal models and clinical studies is required.

item.title: Sequential Therapy with Anlotinib and Radioiodine for Distant Metastatic Differentiated Thyroid Cancer: A Phase II Clinical Trial.
item.dc:creator: Song H, Shen C, Fan Y, Liu Z, Wang Y, Luo Q, Chen L
item.description:
Authors: Song H, Shen C, Fan Y, Liu Z, Wang Y, Luo Q, Chen L
Journal: The oncologist | DOI: 10.1093/oncolo/oyag426
Published: 2026-Oct-22

Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Radioiodine (RAI) alone exhibited limited efficacy in distant metastatic differentiated thyroid cancer (DTC). We hypothesized that pretreatment with anlotinib, a potent antiangiogenic tyrosine kinase inhibitor, would reduce tumor burden and improve therapeutic response. METHODS: This prospective, single-arm phase II trial enrolled patients with measurable distant metastatic DTC. All patients received anlotinib 12 mg/day orally for 12 weeks. After confirmation of RAI-avid target lesions on diagnostic ¹³¹I-WBS, patients were treated with 7.4 GBq RAI and followed up for another 12 weeks. Sequential therapy continued until no effect of RAI could be anticipated. Primary endpoints were objective response rate (ORR) and safety. Registered with the Chinese Clinical Trial Registry (ChiCTR2100045178; https://www.chictr.org.cn). RESULTS: 24 patients were enrolled. 14 (58%) were excluded due to non-RAI-avid target lesions; 10 (42%) with RAI-avid lesions received sequential therapy (median, 4.5 cycles). ORR was 60% (all partial responses), disease control rate 100%. With median follow-up 34.5 months, no disease progression or death occurred. In the subgroup of eight patients with bone target lesions, ORR was 50%. Grade 3 anlotinib-related adverse events occurred in 30% of patients; no grade 4/5 toxicities or grade ≥2 RAI-related events were observed. CONCLUSION: Sequential anlotinib followed by RAI therapy demonstrated promising antitumor activity (ORR 60%) and favorable safety in RAI-avid distant metastatic DTC, particularly in bone metastases. These findings are hypothesis-generating and require validation in a randomized trial with an RAI monotherapy control arm.

Authors: Cabrera CI, Tamaki A, Koroukian SM, Love TE, Singer ME, Teknos TN, Rezaee R, Zhang L
Journal: JAMA otolaryngology-- head & neck surgery | DOI: 10.1001/jamaoto.2026.3290
Published: 2026-Oct-22
PMID: 42911606



Abstract:
IMPORTANCE: Multi-institutional oropharyngeal cancer datasets are increasingly used for research, yet systematic evaluation of data completeness and its clinical impact remains limited. Unrecognized institutional heterogeneity in variable availability, coding conventions, and patient characteristics can introduce substantial bias into combined analyses. OBJECTIVE: To systematically characterize data availability patterns and clinical heterogeneity across 2 major oropharyngeal cancer datasets, evaluate their impact on survival, and develop evidence-based recommendations for multi-institutional research design. DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: A cross-sectional analysis and retrospective cohort study was conducted of the RADCURE dataset (2005-2017) from Princess Margaret Cancer Centre (Toronto, Canada) and the HNSCC-Oropharyngeal dataset (2005-2012) from MD Anderson Cancer Center (Houston, Texas). Patients with complete data on patient and disease characteristics were included. Data were analyzed from 2023 to 2026. EXPOSURES: Institutional dataset, human papillomavirus (HPV) status, tumor (T) stage, node (N) stage, harmonized treatment modality, smoking status, and age at diagnosis. MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: Data completeness rates across clinical and end point variables; overall survival assessed using Kaplan-Meier analysis with Peto-Peto weighted log-rank tests, restricted mean survival time, and multivariable Cox proportional hazards regression stratified by HPV status; machine learning discrimination and calibration for 1-, 5-, and 10-year survival prediction. RESULTS: The final analytic cohort comprised 1972 participants (median [IQR] age, 59.5 [53.4-67.0] years; 347 female [17.6%] and 1625 male [82.4%] individuals), 1482 from the RADCURE and 490 from the HNSCC-Oropharyngeal datasets. Of the total, 1263 had HPV-positive disease (64.0%). Substantial institutional differences were observed across demographic characteristics, HPV distribution, and treatment modality. After comprehensive adjustment, the hazard ratio for treating institutions was 1.19 (95% CI, 0.93-1.52), not excluding a clinically meaningful effect. HPV status violated the proportional hazards assumption, and its prognostic effect was quantified using restricted mean survival time, demonstrating a clinically meaningful survival advantage for patients with HPV-positive disease in both datasets. Machine learning ensemble models achieved moderate to good discrimination (1-year area under the curve [AUC], 0.820; 5-year AUC, 0.777; 10-year AUC 0.786) with institution consistently ranking as a low-importance predictor. CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: In this cross-sectional analysis and cohort study, multi-institutional oropharyngeal cancer datasets exhibited substantial heterogeneity requiring systematic harmonization prior to combined analyses. Systematic harmonization and rigorous assumption testing should be prerequisites for multi-institutional oropharyngeal cancer analyses; after appropriate adjustment, treating institution did not independently predict survival.

item.title: Survivorship Care Before Completion of Definitive Radiotherapy and Oncologic Outcomes in Head and Neck Cancer.
item.dc:creator: Nilsen ML, Carlson KM, Owoc MS, Ashraf R, Bayyoud MI, Hetrick J, Kim S, Zevallos JP, Spector ME, Contrera KJ, et al.
item.description:
Authors: Nilsen ML, Carlson KM, Owoc MS, Ashraf R, Bayyoud MI, Hetrick J, Kim S, Zevallos JP, Spector ME, Contrera KJ, et al.
Journal: JAMA otolaryngology-- head & neck surgery | DOI: 10.1001/jamaoto.2026.3198
Published: 2026-Oct-22
PMID: 42911578



Abstract:
IMPORTANCE: Across cancer populations, a growing and aging survivor population combined with increasing use of multimodal therapy has expanded the need for survivorship care, particularly in head and neck cancer (HNC). Although survivorship begins at diagnosis, survivorship care is often emphasized after treatment completion, and whether earlier integration during treatment is associated with adherence to treatment and survival remains unclear. OBJECTIVE: To evaluate whether early multidisciplinary survivorship care before definitive radiotherapy completion is associated with adherence and survival outcomes. DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: This retrospective cohort study included patients diagnosed with HNC who completed definitive curative-intent radiotherapy at an academic center between March 21, 2018, and March 25, 2025. Patients treated with primary surgery and those receiving palliative-intent radiotherapy were excluded. EXPOSURES: Attendance at a multidisciplinary HNC survivorship clinic before radiotherapy completion. Covariates were sex, race, age and marital status at diagnosis, tumor and nodal categories, history of tobacco or alcohol use, insurance status, treatment with systemic therapy, year of diagnosis, Area Deprivation Index national rank, and cancer site. MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: The primary outcomes were radiotherapy adherence, 3-year recurrence risk, and 3-year disease-free survival (DFS). Radiotherapy adherence was evaluated using logistic regression, DFS using Cox proportional hazards regression, and recurrence using Fine-Gray regression. RESULTS: Among 471 patients in the overall cohort (83 [17.6%] female; 388 [82.4%] male), 148 (31.4%) received early survivorship care, and 247 (52.4%) adhered to radiotherapy. In multivariable analysis adjusting for clinical and sociodemographic factors, attendees had lower odds of radiotherapy nonadherence (odds ratio, 0.45; 95% CI, 0.27-0.75), lower 3-year recurrence risk (subdistribution hazard ratio [SHR], 0.62; 95% CI, 0.40-0.94), and improved 3-year DFS (HR, 0.61; 95% CI, 0.41-0.91). CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: In this study, after adjustment for clinical and sociodemographic factors, early survivorship care was associated with improved radiotherapy adherence and survival among patients with HNC. These findings suggest that earlier integration of multidisciplinary survivorship care, rather than solely after treatment, may be a modifiable care delivery strategy with potential relevance across cancer populations.

item.title: NaV1.8 Inhibition and the Future of Nonopioid Analgesia in Otolaryngology: A Narrative Review.
item.dc:creator: Tham T, Lee JB, Megwalu UC
item.description:
Authors: Tham T, Lee JB, Megwalu UC
Journal: JAMA otolaryngology-- head & neck surgery | DOI: 10.1001/jamaoto.2026.3308
Published: 2026-Oct-22
PMID: 42911570



Abstract:
IMPORTANCE: Postoperative pain management in otolaryngology requires balancing effective analgesia while minimizing adverse effects, such as opioid-related complications. Suzetrigine is a first-in-class selective voltage-gated sodium channel (NaV1.8) inhibitor that has been recently approved by the US Food and Drug Administration. Suzetrigine selectively inhibits NaV1.8 channels expressed in peripheral nociceptive neurons, thereby reducing pain signaling without the respiratory depression, sedation, or misuse potential associated with opioids. This review summarizes the pharmacology, efficacy, safety profile, limitations, and potential applications of suzetrigine in otolaryngology. OBSERVATIONS: Prospective clinical trials consist of 2 phase 2 randomized clinical trials, 2 phase 3 randomized placebo-controlled trials, and 1 phase 3 open-label study involving more than 3000 patients. Across abdominoplasty and bunionectomy pain models, suzetrigine demonstrated superior analgesia compared with placebo and mixed efficacy comparable to hydrocodone/acetaminophen. The drug was generally well tolerated, with adverse event rates similar to placebo and no significant respiratory, cardiac, or sedating adverse effects reported. Additionally, 1 retrospective cohort study has reported results in patients undergoing free flap reconstruction and transoral robotic surgery. CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: Suzetrigine is a promising nonopioid analgesic with demonstrated efficacy compared to placebo in acute postoperative pain and a favorable safety profile. In otolaryngology, suzetrigine may serve as an adjunct to multimodal analgesia and an opioid-sparing option for patients with contraindications to traditional analgesics, opioid use disorder, or procedures that are expected to have high opioid utilization such as tonsillectomy, sleep surgery, and major head and neck surgery. Future studies in otolaryngology are warranted to evaluate whether suzetrigine can meaningfully reduce postoperative opioid exposure without compromising analgesic effectiveness.

item.title: Rituximab vs Azathioprine for Eosinophilic Granulomatosis With Polyangiitis Maintenance Therapy: A Randomized Clinical Trial.
item.dc:creator: Puéchal X, Pugnet G, Thoreau B, de Moreuil C, Jouneau S, Quéméneur T, Baron G, Smets P, Néel A, Le Gallou T, et al.
item.description:
Authors: Puéchal X, Pugnet G, Thoreau B, de Moreuil C, Jouneau S, Quéméneur T, Baron G, Smets P, Néel A, Le Gallou T, et al.
Journal: JAMA | DOI: 10.1001/jama.2026.15278
Published: 2026-Oct-22
PMID: 42911562



Abstract:
IMPORTANCE: For patients with eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA), guidelines recommend considering maintenance therapy after achieving remission. Data comparing maintenance therapeutic options are limited. OBJECTIVE: To compare the effects of rituximab and azathioprine maintenance therapies on remission duration for patients with EGPA who recently achieved remission of vasculitis after standard therapy, including prednisone tapering or withdrawal. DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: From March 7, 2018, to June 2, 2022, this double-blind, double-dummy, investigator-initiated, superiority, randomized clinical trial enrolled 98 participants with EGPA from 36 hospitals in France. Inclusion eligibility required a new EGPA diagnosis or relapsing EGPA within 30 to 360 days of achieving vasculitis remission (Birmingham Vasculitis Activity Score of 0 [range, 0-63, with higher scores indicating more severe disease activity]) after a standard induction regimen. Data were analyzed from April 1, 2025, to September 17, 2025. Additional analyses ended June 22, 2026. INTERVENTIONS: Participants were randomized to receive a predefined standardized tapering of oral prednisone and either 500 mg of intravenous rituximab every 6 months for 18 months and daily oral azathioprine placebo for 24 months (n = 49) or rituximab placebo every 6 months for 18 months and daily oral azathioprine for 24 months (n = 49). MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: The primary efficacy end point was the duration of total remission during the 28-month study period while taking 7.5 mg/d or less of prednisone. The 14 secondary end points included proportion of participants remaining in remission, rate of vasculitis relapse, and rate of asthma or rhinosinusitis exacerbations. RESULTS: All 98 randomized participants (mean age, 59.0 years [SD, 14.4]; 50 women [51%]) received at least 1 dose of the trial regimen and 92 (94%) completed the trial. The mean time in remission with prednisone at 7.5 mg/d or less was 91.1 weeks (95% CI, 80.9-101.2) vs 96.0 weeks (95% CI, 85.6-106.5) in the rituximab and azathioprine groups, respectively (P = .38). The proportion of participants who remained in remission during the 28-month study period with prednisone at 7.5 mg/d or less was 17 of 49 (34.7%) vs 11 of 49 (22.4%; relative risk, 1.51; 95% CI, 0.83-2.73; P = .18) in the rituximab and azathioprine groups, respectively. The proportion of participants with at least 1 vasculitis relapse was 7 (14.3%) vs 9 (18.4%) in the rituximab vs azathioprine groups, respectively, and for those with at least 1 clinically significant asthma exacerbation, rhinosinusitis exacerbation, or both, it was 16 (32.7%) vs 19 (38.8%). One participant in the azathioprine group died of SARS-CoV-2 infection before vaccine development. Rituximab recipients experienced a higher incidence of severe infections (23 [46.9%] vs 12 [24.5%], respectively), primarily due to severe SARS-CoV-2 infections. CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: For participants with newly diagnosed or relapsing EGPA, rituximab was not superior to azathioprine for improving the duration of total remission during 28 months while taking prednisone at 7.5 mg/d or less. TRIAL REGISTRATION: ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT03164473.

item.title: Factors Associated with Adverse Effects of Postoperative TSH-Directed Levothyroxine Therapy in Adults with Differentiated Thyroid Cancer: A Scoping Review.
item.dc:creator: Jay M, Esttaifo F, Reszetnik G, Goens C, Wilson E, Lipscombe LL, Eskander A
item.description:
Authors: Jay M, Esttaifo F, Reszetnik G, Goens C, Wilson E, Lipscombe LL, Eskander A
Journal: Thyroid : official journal of the American Thyroid Association | DOI: 10.1177/10507256261499041
Published: 2026-Oct-22
PMID: 42908960



Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Postoperative thyrotropin (TSH)-directed levothyroxine is used to reduce recurrence risk in selected patients with differentiated thyroid cancer (DTC), but treatment-related adverse effects may vary based on patient susceptibility and treatment exposure. Contemporary guidelines increasingly require balancing anticipated oncologic benefit against potential harm. This scoping review synthesizes patient-, treatment-, and disease-related factors associated with adverse effects of postoperative TSH-directed levothyroxine therapy in adults with DTC. METHODS: This scoping review was reported following PRISMA-ScR guidelines and prospectively registered on the Open Science Framework. MEDLINE, Embase, and Cochrane CENTRAL were searched from January 1, 2011, to February 24, 2026. Eligible studies reported associations between patient-, treatment-, or disease-related factors and adverse effects among adults with DTC receiving postoperative TSH-directed levothyroxine therapy. Data were summarized descriptively and synthesized narratively, with stratification according to TSH exposure definition. RESULTS: Of 7361 records screened, 35 studies including 11,819 patients were included. Skeletal outcomes were most frequently reported (51.4%), followed by cardiometabolic (40.0%), neuropsychological (11.4%), reproductive (2.9%), and muscular outcomes (2.9%). TSH exposure definitions varied substantially: 18 studies evaluated subnormal TSH, 2 low-normal TSH, 8 mixed categories spanning subnormal and low-normal TSH, 4 continuous biochemical/treatment measures, and 3 unclear exposures. Greater suppression intensity was the most consistently reported treatment-related factor associated with adverse skeletal outcomes, particularly in studies evaluating subnormal TSH. Longer treatment duration was associated with skeletal harm in selected studies. Postmenopausal status emerged as a relatively consistent patient-level factor, whereas associations with age and body mass index were variable. Evidence for cardiometabolic, neuropsychological, reproductive, and muscular outcomes was less extensive and less consistent, and disease-related factors were infrequently examined. Only two studies conducted prediction/discrimination analyses, both involving skeletal outcomes. CONCLUSIONS: Evidence on adverse effects associated with TSH-directed levothyroxine therapy in DTC is most consistent for skeletal outcomes and predominantly derives from studies evaluating subnormal TSH exposure. The available literature provides limited evidence for clinically applicable prediction of toxicity or cumulative treatment burden. Future longitudinal studies should better characterize the intensity and persistence of biochemical exposure and develop outcome-specific prediction models integrating baseline susceptibility, organ vulnerability, and longitudinal treatment exposure to support individualized TSH management.

item.title: DNA Adducts, Chromosomal Instability, EMT, and GSTM1 in Oral Squamous Cell Carcinoma.
item.dc:creator: Kheiri SG, Ghodsi K, Tayarani-Najaran Z, Kamelan A
item.description:
Authors: Kheiri SG, Ghodsi K, Tayarani-Najaran Z, Kamelan A
Journal: Oral diseases | DOI: 10.1111/odi.70554
Published: 2026-Oct-22
PMID: 42908337



Abstract:
PURPOSE: To determine whether DNA-adduct burden, chromosomal instability, epithelial-mesenchymal transition, and glutathione S-transferase M1 (GSTM1) genotype are independently associated with advanced-stage oral squamous cell carcinoma or overall survival. METHODS: We studied 160 patients with histologically confirmed oral squamous cell carcinoma. DNA-adduct burden was measured by 32P-postlabeling, validated against mass spectrometry in 50 patients; chromosomal instability by fluorescence in situ hybridization of chromosomes 7, 9, and 11; epithelial-mesenchymal transition by E-cadherin/vimentin immunohistochemistry; and GSTM1 genotype by multiplex polymerase chain reaction. Logistic and Cox regression were performed. RESULTS: DNA-adduct burden and epithelial-mesenchymal transition score were strongly correlated (r = 0.923, p < 0.001), but neither differed by tumor stage. None of the four markers was independently associated with advanced-stage disease. During follow-up, 48 patients died. Nodal positivity (hazard ratio 3.84, 95% confidence interval 2.00-7.38, p < 0.001) and Stage IV disease (hazard ratio 7.82, 95% confidence interval 2.12-28.84, p = 0.002) were independently associated with poorer survival. The combined clinical-molecular model showed modest discrimination (AUC 0.689). CONCLUSION: Nodal status and advanced stage were the dominant independent determinants of survival, with routine nodal assessment improving prognostic discrimination beyond stage alone. The four molecular markers tracked with disease characteristics but added no independent prognostic value, warranting replication in larger, prospective cohorts.

item.title: RIPK3 Promotes Gingival Fibroblast Apoptosis and Periodontal Inflammatory Injury by Impairing Mitophagy.
item.dc:creator: Huang Y, Zhou Y, Li S, Zhang Y, Lan Y, Li W, Guo L
item.description:
Authors: Huang Y, Zhou Y, Li S, Zhang Y, Lan Y, Li W, Guo L
Journal: Oral diseases | DOI: 10.1111/odi.70555
Published: 2026-Oct-21
PMID: 42908318



Abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Periodontitis drives persistent inflammation, alveolar bone loss, mitochondrial dysfunction and fibroblast programmed cell death. Receptor-interacting protein kinase 3 (RIPK3) regulates inflammation and cell fate, while its role in modulating FUNDC1-associated mitophagy and cell death in periodontitis remains poorly defined. METHODS: Clinical gingival tissues, a ligature-induced rat periodontitis model, and Pg.LPS-stimulated human gingival fibroblasts were used. RIPK3 function was verified via pharmacological inhibition and siRNA-mediated knockdown, combined with mitophagy intervention and detection of mitochondrial damage, apoptosis and necroptosis. RESULTS: RIPK3 and pTyr18-FUNDC1 were upregulated while LC3-II was downregulated in periodontitis tissues. RIPK3 inhibition restored defective mitophagic flux, alleviated mitochondrial dysfunction, apoptosis and MLKL-mediated necroptosis. Mitophagy activation reversed LPS-induced injuries, whereas autophagy inhibition abrogated RIPK3-related protection. RIPK3 acts as an upstream regulator of FUNDC1 Tyr18 phosphorylation, without confirming direct catalytic activity or specific FUNDC1 dependency. CONCLUSION: RIPK3 elevation exacerbates periodontal damage via mitophagy impairment and dual activation of apoptosis and necroptosis. RIPK3 inhibition improves mitophagy, though its direct targeting of FUNDC1 requires further validation. RIPK3 serves as a promising therapeutic candidate for periodontitis.

item.title: Oncologic Outcomes and Treatment Feasibility of Transoral Carbon Dioxide Laser Microsurgery for Hypopharyngeal Tumors in Older Patients: A Retrospective Cohort Study.
item.dc:creator: Ono T, Chitose SI, Kurita T, Sato F, Fukahori M, Sueyoshi S, Kawaguchi T, Oka T, Kuroiwa T, Umeno H
item.description:
Authors: Ono T, Chitose SI, Kurita T, Sato F, Fukahori M, Sueyoshi S, Kawaguchi T, Oka T, Kuroiwa T, Umeno H
Journal: Head & neck | DOI: 10.1002/hed.70523
Published: 2026-Oct-21
PMID: 42908194



Abstract:
BACKGROUND: We evaluated outcomes and complications of transoral CO2 laser microsurgery (TLM) for hypopharyngeal tumors and its feasibility in ≥ 75-year-old patients. METHODS: We retrospectively reviewed 116 patients (without metastases) treated from February 2012 to October 2024 at our hospital. Oncologic outcomes were analyzed using Kaplan-Meier curves (110 patients; median follow-up: 5.3 years). RESULTS: Five-year local control, disease-specific survival, and overall survival rates were 87.8%, 94.6%, and 85.6%, respectively. Postoperative dysphagia, aspiration pneumonia, pharyngolaryngeal edema, and vocal fold paralysis occurred in 9%, 4%, 3%, and 3% of patients, respectively; none required tracheostomy or surgical hemostasis under general anesthesia. The group with a history of head and neck irradiation had higher rates of dysphagia (p = 0.010) and aspiration pneumonia (p = 0.031) than those without. Differences between age groups were nonsignificant. CONCLUSIONS: TLM appears safe and effective for older patients with appropriately selected hypopharyngeal tumors.

item.title: Comparison of Stress-Mediated Vocal Fold Epithelial Effects in Conventionally-Raised and Germ-Free Mice.
item.dc:creator: Venkatraman A, Jacobs K, Thibeault SL
item.description:
Authors: Venkatraman A, Jacobs K, Thibeault SL
Journal: The Laryngoscope | DOI: 10.1002/lary.71008
Published: 2026-Oct-21
PMID: 42907181



Abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Up to 25% of patients with voice disorders report concurrent psychosocial stress, which has been shown to cause laryngeal microbiome dysbiosis. Microbiome dysbiosis underlies disease pathophysiology in other organs, leading to uncontrolled inflammation via epithelial barrier dysfunction. There is a need to delineate microbial versus nonmicrobial epithelial stress pathways in the vocal folds (VF) in order to clarify how psychosocial stress may contribute to VF epithelial disease. METHODS: C57BL/6 conventionally-raised (CR) and germ-free (GF) adult mice were equally allocated to stressed and unstressed groups (n = 64, 32 per mouse-type/group, equal sexes). Stressed animals completed a validated restraint stress protocol. Following stress, larynges were collected. Outcomes of VF epithelial barrier dysfunction were compared across stressed, unstressed GF, and CR mice. Immunofluorescence/Immunohistochemistry determined protein expression of epithelial adherens junctions, mucins, and proliferation in mid-membranous VF tissue. Transmission electron microscopy assessed VF epithelial permeability. RESULTS: Regardless of microbiota status, stressed animals had reduced protein expression of VF epithelial adherens junctions, mucins (MUC1, 4) and increased epithelial permeability. Presence of microbiota was associated with stress-induced increases epithelial proliferation, observed in CR, but not GF mice. CONCLUSION: Presence of microbiota was associated with stress-induced increase in VF epithelial proliferation. This increased proliferation may represent an adaptive response to damaged cells to maintain epithelial integrity. Collectively, these findings provide a foundation for identifying VF epithelial targets that could be leveraged in probiotic-based therapies. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: N/A.

item.title: A Clinical Study of 66 Cases of Sinonasal Malignant Lymphoma: Results of a Single-Institution Study.
item.dc:creator: Inomata K, Naito S, Takayama N, Fujiwara M, Matsumoto Y, Yokoi H
item.description:
Authors: Inomata K, Naito S, Takayama N, Fujiwara M, Matsumoto Y, Yokoi H
Journal: The Laryngoscope | DOI: 10.1002/lary.71010
Published: 2026-Oct-21
PMID: 42907180



Abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Early diagnosis and treatment of sinonasal malignant lymphoma are crucial because of its diverse clinical and imaging findings and poor prognosis associated with certain histological subtypes. However, the markers that predict the diagnosis and prognosis according to the histological subtypes are unclear. This study aimed to identify these markers. METHODS: We retrospectively analyzed 66 malignant lymphomas diagnosed using biopsy specimens obtained from the nasal cavity and sinus and treated at our institution. Age, sex, main symptom, primary site, disease stage, histopathological type, blood test parameters, follow-up period, treatment details, and prognosis were analyzed. Overall survival was defined as the time from diagnosis to death from any cause. Progression-free survival was defined as the time from diagnosis to disease progression, relapse, or death. Survival curves were estimated using the Kaplan-Meier method and compared using the log-rank test. RESULTS: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) was the most common histological subtype (45 patients), followed by extranodal natural killer (NK)/T-cell lymphoma (ENKTL; 15 patients). The 5-year progression-free survival rates were 50.0% for DLBCL and ENKTL for 28.1%. ENKTL was associated with a significantly poorer prognosis than DLBCL. Among patients with sinonasal DLBCL, CD5-positivity tended to have a poorer prognosis. CONCLUSION: Sinonasal malignant lymphoma exhibits heterogeneous clinical behavior according to the histological subtype. CD5-positive sinonasal DLBCL tended to result in worse outcomes. To our knowledge, this is the first study to investigate the prognostic significance of CD5 expression in sinonasal DLBCL. Further studies are needed to clarify its prognostic significance.

item.title: Oncologic Outcomes in p16-Positive Oropharyngeal Squamous Cell Carcinoma With Extranodal Extension.
item.dc:creator: Taylor V, MacKay C, Taylor SM, Trites J, Al Afif A, Mendez A, Rigby MH
item.description:
Authors: Taylor V, MacKay C, Taylor SM, Trites J, Al Afif A, Mendez A, Rigby MH
Journal: The Laryngoscope | DOI: 10.1002/lary.71006
Published: 2026-Oct-21
PMID: 42907157



Abstract:
OBJECTIVES: Treatment de-escalation in HPV-associated oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma (OPSCC) is controversial when extranodal extension (ENE) is present. This study evaluated whether pathologic ENE (pENE) presence and extent (microscopic vs. macroscopic) affect survival outcomes in p16-positive OPSCC treated with primary surgery. METHODS: This single-center retrospective cohort included patients with p16-positive OPSCC treated surgically with or without adjuvant treatment from September 2014 to July 2024. Outcomes included overall (OS), disease-specific (DSS), and disease-free survival (DFS). Kaplan-Meier survival curves were compared between groups using log-rank tests. Multivariable analyses used LASSO-selected variables. RESULTS: Among 232 patients, pENE status was reported in 216, forming the primary multivariable cohort. pENE was present in 115 (53.2%); 69.6% were macroscopic. Five-year OS, DSS, and DFS for the full cohort were 88.5%, 94.4%, and 89.0%, respectively. pENE positivity was not significantly associated with DSS (93.3% vs. 94.6%, p = 0.86), DFS (87.7% vs. 91.7%, p = 0.46), or OS (83.2% vs. 93.4%, p = 0.052). Within pENE-positive disease, 5-year OS was 89.8% for microscopic versus 80.2% for macroscopic pENE (p = 0.22). On complete-case adjusted analysis (N = 96), macroscopic pENE had a nonsignificant 3.8-fold higher hazard of death (HR = 3.77, p = 0.063). Exploratory risk-gradient analysis showed worse OS with macroscopic pENE (HR = 3.29, p = 0.046) and clinical ENE (cENE; HR = 5.07, p = 0.040) compared to a pENE-negative/microscopic pENE reference. CONCLUSION: Macroscopic pENE showed a directional association with worse OS, and exploratory analyses suggested a possible risk-gradient with increasing severity from microscopic pENE to cENE. Larger studies are required to determine the clinical significance of pENE extent in surgically treated HPV-associated OPSCC.

item.title: Planned versus accumulated dose in radiotherapy of oropharyngeal carcinoma - Do recurrences occur in unintended cold spots?
item.dc:creator: Lindegaard AM, Enocson H, Georgiev H, Appelt A, Bernsdorf M, Gothelf A, Kristensen CA, Petersen J, Specht L, Tavlayan E, et al.
item.description:
Authors: Lindegaard AM, Enocson H, Georgiev H, Appelt A, Bernsdorf M, Gothelf A, Kristensen CA, Petersen J, Specht L, Tavlayan E, et al.
Journal: Radiotherapy and oncology : journal of the European Society for Therapeutic Radiology and Oncology | DOI: 10.1016/j.radonc.2026.111830
Published: 2026-Oct-21
PMID: 42906639



Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Locoregional recurrence (LRR) in oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma (OPSCC) patients treated with radiotherapy (RT) most often occurs within the high-dose target volume. Anatomical changes during RT may potentially lead to unintended target underdosage, which could contribute to the risk of treatment failure. This study aimed to quantify differences between planned and accumulated dose in the regions of later LRR. METHODS: Patients treated with curatively intended RT for OPSCC between 2009 and 2017 at Rigshospitalet with biopsy-proven LRR were identified. Recurrence volumes were delineated on follow up imaging and mapped to the planning CT. The point of origin (PO) of each recurrence was determined using the nidus method. Dose accumulation was performed using synthetic CTs based on daily cone beam CT, followed by recalculation and summation of daily dose distributions. Planned and accumulated doses at the PO were compared. Additional analyses evaluated effect of deformable registration methods. RESULTS: Forty patients with 54 recurrence volumes were included. The accumulated dose was higher than the planned dose in 57% of recurrences. The mean difference between accumulated and planned dose at the PO was - 0.04 Gy (SD: 0.81; 95% CI: -0.26 to 0.18 Gy; p = 0.72). Neither PO localization nor the dose accumulation process was sensitive to the use of an alternative deformation software. CONCLUSIONS: Within the evaluated setting, no evidence was found that regions of later LRR were systematically underdosed. Dose differences were small and within clinically acceptable limits. This suggests that anatomical changes during RT were unlikely to cause clinically relevant compromised target dose coverage.

item.title: Predicting taste alteration in head and neck cancer patients using 3D transformer-based deep learning model.
item.dc:creator: Neh H, MacRae DC, de Vette SPM, van der Hoek L, van Ooijen PMA, Sijtsema NM, Langendijk JA, van Dijk LV
item.description:
Authors: Neh H, MacRae DC, de Vette SPM, van der Hoek L, van Ooijen PMA, Sijtsema NM, Langendijk JA, van Dijk LV
Journal: Oral oncology | DOI: 10.1016/j.oraloncology.2026.108192
Published: 2026-Oct-21
PMID: 42906280



Abstract:
PURPOSE: Taste alteration is a common post-treatment side effect of head and neck cancer (HNC) radiotherapy. Accurate normal tissue complication probability (NTCP) models can support treatment planning aimed at reducing side effects that impair quality-of-life. Deep learning (DL) offers opportunities to incorporate full 3D dose, CT, and organofinterest (OOI) data. Using a large prospective cohort, this study explores whether CNN and transformerbased DL models can outperform a conventional logistic regression model for predicting taste alteration 6 months after radiotherapy. MATERIAL/METHODS: Data from 972 patients was used, with the endpoint being moderatetosevere patientreported taste alteration at six months (EORTC QLQH&N35). DL models were trained using 3D dose distributions, planning CT, OOI segmentations and clinical features. A conventional NTCP model using oral cavity mean dose, parotid mean dose, and age served as reference. Attention maps were evaluated for the transformer-based DL model to quantify the model attention to specific regions of the head and neck area. In addition, two cropping approaches for the 3D data were compared. RESULTS: The CNN and transformer DL models performed comparable to the reference NTCP model in the test set (Reference: AUC = 0.71; ResNet: AUC = 0.68; TransRP: AUC = 0.71), though calibration was best for the reference model. Shifting the crop improved DL performance and transformer attention focused on supraglottic and submandibular regions. CONCLUSION: This study showed that the prediction of taste alteration can be achieved using DL models, particularly transformer-based models which, in contrast to CNNs, can account for global features of comprehensive 3D information of dose distribution, CT-images and organs-of-interest segmentations.

item.title: Toward vestibule-specific staging in nasal vestibule squamous cell carcinoma: a single-centre cohort study.
item.dc:creator: Berardinis R, Durante S, Riccio S, Vavassori A, Tagliabue M, Colombi L, Onza M, Giugliano G, Bruschini R, Ruju F, et al.

Authors: Berardinis R, Durante S, Riccio S, Vavassori A, Tagliabue M, Colombi L, Onza M, Giugliano G, Bruschini R, Ruju F, et al.

Published: 2026-Oct-21
